opus-5.5.text:
I think of responsible scaling policies as a kind of first draft, a way for labs to start doing this before regulation exists, and hopefully to inform what good regulation could eventually look like. When we wrote ours, part of the motivation was that the technology is moving really fast and governments take time. Someone has to work out in practice what it means to evaluate a model for dangerous capabilities, what safeguards you'd want at different risk levels, and how you'd commit in advance to pausing or adding protections if you hit certain thresholds. Labs are well placed to do that experimentation because we have the models and can try things out and learn what's workable.

But I don't think voluntary commitments from individual companies are a sufficient end state. There are a few problems. One is that not every developer will adopt them, or adopt strong versions of them. If only some labs are cautious, you get competitive pressure, where the careful lab feels it's falling behind. Another is accountability. Even if a company means well, there's a real question of why the public should trust it to grade its own homework. You want external verification, and ultimately you want something with legal teeth.

So the ideal trajectory, as I see it, is that RSPs act as a testing ground. Different labs try different approaches, we learn which evaluations actually track risk, which commitments are realistic, and where the thresholds should sit, and that accumulated experience gives policymakers something concrete to build on. Over time I'd like to see the core ideas become regulation: if your model reaches certain capability levels, you have to meet certain safety and security standards, with independent checks that you're actually doing it.

The nice thing about the framework is that it's conditional. It doesn't say "stop AI development" or "do nothing." It says the requirements should scale with the risk, and I think that's something people with quite different views on how dangerous AI is can get behind. If you think the risks are far off, the requirements won't bind for a while. If you think they're close, the commitments kick in soon. That makes it a reasonable basis for policy, because you don't have to settle every disagreement about timelines up front to agree on the structure.

r001.rationale: It says voluntary commitments are insufficient because not every developer will adopt them, and calls for capability-triggered legal standards, addressing the gap left by non-adopters.

r002.rationale: It describes labs testing different approaches and accumulating evidence about evaluations, commitments, and thresholds for policymakers to build on when designing regulation.

fable-5.1.text:
Yeah, so I think the way I'd frame it is that responsible scaling policies are not a substitute for regulation. They're more like a precursor to it, or a way of figuring out what good regulation might eventually look like.

The basic idea behind an RSP is that you tie your safety and security commitments to specific capability thresholds. So you say, if a model can do X, then before we train or deploy it we need to have Y safeguards in place. And the reason that structure is appealing is that it doesn't require you to predict exactly when dangerous capabilities arrive. You just commit to having evaluations that would catch them, and to not proceeding until you've met the bar.

Now, the obvious limitation is that these are voluntary. A company can write one, and a company can change it. We've tried to make ours hard to walk back on, but at the end of the day it's a commitment a company is making about itself, and I think people are right to be somewhat skeptical of that. It's not what you'd want as the final state of the world.

So where I see regulation coming in is basically taking the parts of these policies that turn out to work and making them mandatory across the industry. Right now there's a lot of uncertainty about what the right evaluations are, what the right thresholds are, what safeguards are actually effective. Companies that are building these models have a lot of the information needed to answer those questions. If a few labs run these policies for a while, and some of them turn out to be reasonable and some turn out to be badly calibrated, that's useful evidence for policymakers who otherwise would be writing rules somewhat blind.

There's also a coordination problem that RSPs can't solve on their own. If one lab says "we won't proceed past this threshold without these safeguards" and another lab just goes ahead, the first lab has mostly handicapped itself. Regulation is what makes the commitment apply to everyone, so you're not relying on every single actor being well-intentioned.

I'd also say there's a risk in the other direction, which is that regulation gets written too early, locks in a particular set of tests that don't track real risk, and then everyone's complying with the letter of something that's not actually making things safer. So I don't think the answer is just "regulate now, in detail." I think it's more that the voluntary commitments should be seen as a draft, and the goal should be to move the good parts into something enforceable as quickly as we can do that well.

r001.rationale: The response describes the coordination gap when one lab makes an RSP commitment but another lab proceeds anyway, and says regulation should make commitments apply to everyone.

r002.rationale: It says companies’ trials of RSPs can reveal which evaluations, thresholds, and safeguards work, giving policymakers evidence to inform regulation.

astra-6.text:
I think responsible scaling policies can be a useful starting point for regulation. The basic idea is that, as models become more capable, there should be explicit thresholds at which you need stronger safeguards—or you shouldn’t continue scaling or deploying until you have those safeguards in place.

Having companies develop these policies lets us learn something about what those thresholds should be, how to evaluate whether a model has crossed them, and what safeguards are actually feasible. There’s a lot we don’t know yet, so being able to iterate on that is valuable.

But voluntary policies aren’t enough. You want government to establish a floor that applies across companies, including companies that wouldn’t voluntarily adopt a strong policy. And you need some way to verify that companies are actually doing what they say they’re doing.

So I see these as complementary. Companies can help develop and test the approaches, but government needs to decide which requirements should be binding. The challenge is making those requirements concrete enough to be enforceable while keeping them adaptable as our understanding of the risks improves.

r001.rationale: It says a government floor should cover companies that would not voluntarily adopt a strong policy.

r002.rationale: It says companies’ policy development and testing can reveal useful thresholds and feasible safeguards, which can inform the binding requirements government designs.

sol-6.1.text:
I think responsible scaling policies can be a useful starting point for regulation. The basic idea is that, as models become more capable, the safeguards you need should become stronger. You identify capabilities that could create serious risks, evaluate whether your models have those capabilities, and commit in advance to what you’ll do if they do — including not proceeding until you have adequate safeguards.

Companies can start doing that voluntarily, which helps us learn what evaluations and safeguards actually work. But voluntary commitments aren’t a sufficient long-term solution. You want some way to ensure that every company developing sufficiently powerful systems meets an appropriate standard, even when doing so is commercially inconvenient.

I’d like regulation to preserve the ability to update the technical details as we learn more, while making the obligations meaningful. That could mean requiring companies to have a policy, evaluate their systems, and provide enough independent oversight that we can tell whether they’re following it. The hard part is making sure this becomes a real constraint on dangerous development, rather than just a requirement to produce a document.

r001.rationale: The response says voluntary commitments are insufficient and that regulation should ensure every company developing sufficiently powerful systems meets an appropriate standard, identifying the coverage gap regulation must address.

r002.rationale: It says voluntary implementation can help reveal which evaluations and safeguards work, connecting that evidence to the later discussion of regulatory standards and oversight.
